opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of those things that sounds like a minor knob, but in practice it ends up being one of the most consequential decisions in the whole auto-labeling pipeline.

When you use a foundation model to pre-label a dataset, every prediction comes with a confidence score, and you have to decide where to cut. If you set the threshold too high, you're very conservative: the labels you keep are mostly correct, but you miss a lot of true objects. Your recall drops, and the downstream model learns that those missed objects are background. That's a subtle failure, because the data looks clean when you inspect it, but you've baked false negatives into your training set.

If you go too low, you pull in many more of the true positives, but you also get a lot of junk: duplicate boxes, hallucinated objects, mislabeled classes. Then either a human has to clean that up, which undercuts the cost savings that motivated auto-labeling, or the noise flows into training.

What we've found, and I think this surprises some people, is that the best threshold for training a downstream model isn't necessarily the one that maximizes some label-quality metric like F1 against ground truth. Moderate thresholds often do better than very high ones, because recall matters more for downstream training than intuition suggests. A slightly noisy but more complete label set can beat a pristine but sparse one.

The other practical point is that there's no universal number. The right threshold depends on the foundation model, how well its pretraining aligns with your domain, the class you're labeling, and even how calibrated the model is. Rare or visually ambiguous classes behave very differently from common ones. So we encourage people to treat the threshold as a hyperparameter to tune empirically: label a small validated subset, sweep thresholds, train downstream, and see what actually performs, rather than picking 0.5 or 0.9 out of habit.

And finally, confidence is a great signal for routing human attention. Instead of one hard cutoff, you can have bands: accept the high-confidence labels automatically, discard the very low ones, and send the uncertain middle to human reviewers. That's where you get most of the value. You keep the cost advantage of auto-labeling while concentrating your human effort where the model is genuinely unsure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think confidence thresholds are one of those things that sound like a small implementation detail but actually end up being the hinge that the whole auto-labeling workflow turns on. The reality is that a foundation model is going to give you an answer for every single sample you throw at it. It doesn't abstain on its own. So the question isn't really "can the model label this," it's "which of these labels do I trust enough to let through without a human looking at them," and the threshold is where you encode that decision.

A couple of things I'd say about it from a practical standpoint. First, the raw confidence score coming out of these models is not well calibrated, and it's especially not calibrated on your data. These models were trained on a distribution that is probably quite different from a factory floor or a specific medical imaging setup or whatever your domain is. So if you take a score of 0.9 at face value and assume that means ninety percent of those labels are correct, you're going to be surprised. We've seen cases where the model is extremely confident and extremely wrong, and it's systematically wrong on a particular slice of the data, which is the worst case because those errors are correlated and they'll propagate straight into the model you're training downstream.

So what I actually think matters is treating the threshold as something you measure rather than something you pick. You hold out a small, carefully labeled set, you look at how precision moves as you sweep the threshold, and you set it based on the cost of a wrong label in your application versus the cost of sending something to a human. For some tasks a few percent noise in the labels is fine, the downstream training is robust to it. For others, say a safety-critical detection task, you want a very high bar and you accept that most of the volume still gets routed to review.

The second thing is that the threshold shouldn't be a single global number. Confidence behaves differently across classes, across lighting conditions, across whatever the axes of variation are in your data. The really valuable thing a threshold does is give you a triage mechanism: the high confidence stuff flows through, the low confidence stuff is obviously going to a person, and that middle band is where the interesting data lives. That's often where the model is struggling, where your edge cases are, and honestly where your human labeling budget has the most leverage.

So I'd say the practical importance is high, but not because of the number itself. It's important because it forces you to be explicit about how much you trust the model, and to build a loop where that trust is checked against reality rather than assumed. If you skip that step, auto-labeling just becomes a fast way to bake the foundation model's mistakes into your own.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very important, but a confidence threshold is only useful if the confidence actually means something. A foundation model can give you a prediction that looks very confident and still be wrong, particularly when your data differs from what it was trained on. So I wouldn’t take a score of 0.9 and assume that means the label has a 90 percent chance of being correct.

Practically, you need to validate that on a representative sample of your own data. Then you can decide which predictions to accept automatically and which to send to a person for review. Raise the threshold and you’ll generally get fewer automatic labels, but better quality. Lower it and you get more coverage, with more mistakes.

And that tradeoff depends on the task. Missing a rare but important object may be much more costly than getting a common category wrong. So I see thresholds as part of a quality-control process, alongside human review and ongoing measurement, rather than a single setting that makes auto-labeling trustworthy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re incredibly important, but a confidence threshold by itself isn’t enough. The practical question is: how much of the data can I label automatically while maintaining the quality I need? If I set the threshold very high, I may get very good labels, but only on a small fraction of my data. If I lower it, I get more coverage, but I’m also introducing more errors.

And the model’s confidence isn’t necessarily a calibrated probability that the label is correct. You need to validate that relationship on data representative of your application, potentially on a per-class basis. Then you can use the threshold to decide which labels to accept automatically and which examples to send to a person for review. That’s where it becomes useful operationally: managing the tradeoff between annotation effort and label quality.
